title: Step 1: Hook - The Magic of Changes
text: Imagine you are making a roti. First, you roll out the dough into a circle. If the shape is not perfect, you can easily roll it back into a ball of dough. But once you bake that roti on a hot tawa, can you turn it back into dough? The world around us is full of changes, some temporary and some permanent. Let's explore this mystery!

title: Step 2: Socratic Thinking
text: Why do you think some things can go back to how they were before, but other things change forever? What makes the baked roti fundamentally different from the rolled dough?

content.title: Step 3: Discovery - Melting Ice vs Burning Wood
content.description: Notice how ice turning into water can be reversed by cooling. But wood turning into ash cannot be reversed.

title: Step 4: The Reveal - Reversible and Irreversible Changes
text: Changes that can be undone to get back the original substance are called **Reversible Changes** (like melting ice or folding a paper). Changes that cannot be undone are called **Irreversible Changes** (like baking a cake, burning wood, or growing taller).

content.title: Teacher's Tip
content.text: To remember this, think of the word 'Reverse'. A car can go in reverse gear to go back. If a change can go in 'reverse', it's Reversible!

question: Which of the following is an irreversible change?

content.title: Common Mistake: Breaking Glass
content.text: Students often think that breaking a glass is a reversible change because you still have glass pieces. But you cannot easily join them back to form the original glass! It is an irreversible change.

title: Step 6: Reflection
text: Think about your own body. Your height increases as you grow, and your nails grow longer. Are these changes reversible? Try explaining this concept to your younger sibling or a friend in your own words.

title: Step 7: Connection
text: This connects directly to what we will learn in Chemistry. Reversible changes are often 'Physical Changes' (state or shape changes), while irreversible changes are often 'Chemical Changes' where a completely new substance is formed!

content.title: Step 8: Mastery - The Change Hunt
content.description: Walk around your house and list 5 changes you see happening. Classify them into Reversible or Irreversible. For example: Drying wet clothes (Reversible), Rusting of an iron nail (Irreversible).

title: Step 1: Hook - The Mystery of the Bullock Cart Wheel
text: Have you noticed that wooden doors sometimes get stuck and are hard to close during summer, but they work fine in winter? Or how a blacksmith fits a tight iron rim over a larger wooden wheel of a bullock cart? How is that possible?

title: Step 2: Socratic Thinking
text: If metal is hard and solid, how can the blacksmith change its size to make it fit over the wooden wheel without breaking it?

content.title: Step 3: Discovery - Heating and Cooling Metals
content.description: Observe how heating the iron ring makes it slightly larger, allowing it to slip over the wooden wheel. Pouring cold water makes it shrink and grip the wheel tightly.

title: Step 4: The Reveal - Expansion and Contraction
text: When a substance is heated, its size increases. This process is called **Expansion**. When it cools down, its size decreases back to normal. This is called **Contraction**.

question: What happens to the iron rim of a bullock cart wheel when it is heated?
options: It expands and its size increases
It contracts and its size decreases

title: Step 6: Reflection
text: Have you ever struggled to open a tight jar lid? Have you seen adults pour hot water over the metal lid to open it? Think about why that works using the concepts of expansion and contraction.

title: Step 7: Connection
text: This connects to the 'Heat' and 'States of Matter' chapters. When objects are heated, the tiny particles inside them get more energy and spread out, causing expansion.

content.title: Step 8: Mastery - The Balloon Experiment
content.description: Mini-challenge: Stretch a balloon over the mouth of an empty glass bottle. Place the bottle in a bowl of hot water and observe the balloon. Then place it in cold water. See expansion and contraction in action!
